title: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure

questions.stem: A child with CFTR ΔF508 has no chloride channel at the apical membrane of airway cells, although the mutant protein can still conduct chloride. What happens to the mutant protein?

options.A: It lacks mannose-6-phosphate and is secreted
options.B: It is retained in the ER and degraded (ERAD)
options.C: It is never translated on ER-bound ribosomes
options.D: It is imported into peroxisomes by an SKL signal
options.E: It is retrieved from the Golgi by a KDEL signal

questions.explanation: ΔF508 CFTR is misfolded but functional; ER quality control retains it and degrades it (ERAD), so it never reaches the apical membrane. A: Missing M6P with secretion of the enzymes is I-cell disease. C: CFTR is a membrane protein, made on ER-bound ribosomes. D: SKL targets cytosolic proteins to peroxisomes. E: KDEL retrieval applies to ER-resident proteins, not CFTR.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slide 23

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy, developmentally normal until age 6, has progressive loss of vision, hearing and motor skills, with adrenal insufficiency. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are elevated. What is the primary defect?
questions.explanation: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: ABCD1 mutation impairs peroxisomal oxidation of VLCFAs, which accumulate in the nervous system and adrenals; onset at 5–10 years. A: Biogenesis defects (Zellweger) present in infancy and are fatal in the first year. B: Mistargeting of lysosomal enzymes is I-cell disease. C: mtDNA disorders are maternally inherited and don't raise VLCFAs. D: CPT-I carries long-chain, not very-long-chain, fatty acids and causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slides 32–34

questions.stem: A mitochondrial myopathy affects a mother and all her children with very different severity. Which statement best explains this pattern?

options.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
options.D: Mutation in a nuclear gene encoding a mitochondrial protein

questions.explanation: mtDNA comes from the oocyte; differing proportions of mutant mtDNA (heteroplasmy) cause variable severity. B: Would allow paternal transmission. C: Lyonization applies to X-linked genes. D: Nuclear-encoded defects follow Mendelian inheritance. E: Imprinting involves parent-specific gene silencing, not mtDNA.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slide 27

questions.stem: A 2-month-old has hypotonia, seizures, dysmorphic features and an enlarged liver. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids and phytanic acid are elevated, and plasmalogens are low. What is the underlying defect?
questions.explanation: Zellweger syndrome: without functional peroxisomes, VLCFA and phytanic acid oxidation, plasmalogen and bile acid synthesis all fail; fatal in the first year. A: X-ALD affects VLCFA transport only and starts at 5–10 years. B: Refsum disease raises phytanic acid alone, with onset in childhood or adolescence. C: Acid α-glucosidase deficiency is Pompe disease (lysosomal glycogen). D: This is I-cell disease (lysosomal enzyme mistargeting).
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slides 32, 35

questions.stem: A patient receiving paclitaxel develops neutropenia. How does paclitaxel arrest dividing cells?
questions.explanation: Taxanes stabilize microtubules, freezing the mitotic spindle. A: Blocking polymerization is vincristine/vinblastine (and colchicine). C: Actin isn't the target. D: Dynein isn't directly inhibited. E: Intermediate filaments aren't targeted.

questions.stem: A protein is made with an N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence and a KDEL sequence near its C-terminus. Where will it finally reside?
questions.explanation: The signal sequence brings it into the ER on ER-bound ribosomes; KDEL keeps it in the ER or returns it from the Golgi. A: Lysosomal proteins need mannose-6-phosphate. B: Peroxisomal proteins carry SKL and are made on free ribosomes. C: Secreted proteins also start with a signal sequence, but KDEL retains this one. E: Nuclear proteins use basic NLS sequences and are made on free ribosomes.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has coarse facial features, restricted joint movement, and developmental delay. Plasma levels of multiple lysosomal hydrolases are markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: I-cell disease: no mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted into plasma. A: Tay-Sachs. B: Gaucher. D: Hurler. E: Pompe. None of these raise plasma levels of multiple hydrolases.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent otitis media, and bloody diarrhea. Platelets are low and small. His maternal uncle had similar problems. Which cellular process is defective?
questions.explanation: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (X-linked, WAS protein) disrupts actin organization in blood cells: eczema, infections, thrombocytopenia with small platelets. A: Microtubule defects don't give this triad. B: Dynein defects cause Kartagener syndrome. C: Keratin defects cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex. E: Mistargeting causes I-cell disease.

questions.stem: A lab uses fluorescent annexin V to identify apoptotic cells in culture. What does annexin V binding detect?

options.A: Phosphatidylcholine moved to the inner leaflet
options.C: Phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer leaflet

questions.explanation: PS is normally kept in the inner leaflet by ATP-dependent flippases; its exposure on the outer leaflet is the "eat-me" signal of apoptotic cells, detected with annexin V. A: PC is normally in the outer leaflet; its position isn't the marker. B: Raft cholesterol isn't what annexin V binds. D: Phospholipase C (e.g., C. perfringens alpha toxin) lyses membranes; it isn't an apoptosis marker. E: PI signaling happens on the inner leaflet.

questions.stem: How does cholesterol affect the fluidity of the plasma membrane?

options.A: Less fluid at body temperature; prevents freezing at low temperature
options.B: More fluid at body temperature; tighter packing at low temperature
options.E: No effect on fluidity; it only forms lipid rafts

questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: at body temperature it restricts tail movement (less fluid, less permeable), and at low temperature it prevents tight packing. B: That reverses both effects. C: Cis-unsaturated tails and ethanol increase fluidity; cholesterol doesn't. D: At low temperature it keeps the membrane from freezing. E: Rafts are one role, but cholesterol also buffers fluidity.
